newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigeria shuts down for test-case election.
newsitem.headline: Nigeria shuts down for test-case election.

text.p: Shops and businesses closed across Nigeria and the streets of major cities were deserted on Saturday during voting in local elections seen as a test of the military's commitment to return the African nation to democracy.

Authorities ordered all transport off the roads for the polling period from 8 a.m. (0700 GMT) to 4 p.m (1500 GMT) to ensure people go to polling stations, which are supposed to be within walking distance for all voters.
Voting started off on time but slowly in Nigeria's commercial capital Lagos, a centre of opposition to military rule since the army aborted an earlier democracy programme nearly four years ago.

"I am here to vote because I want democracy to come back so the economy will be better," said Benjamin Otobo, the first voter on the queue at St Peter's Church polling station in the commercial district of Lagos.
At several polling stations in middle class districts of Lagos, officials sat at their tables with no sign of voters, but poll inspectors said they expected turnout to pick up.
Enthusiasm was markedly higher in poorer neighbourhoods.

Polling in the capital Abuja started on schedule but rowdy scenes erupted at some polling stations where voters complained their names were missing from voter lists or that numbers on their cards did not match those on the register.
"I was registered here as voter number two but now my name is not on the list. I must vote," said voter John Dare at the NYSC polling station in the capital's Area 2.
The poll to elect chairmen and councillors to more than 770 town halls is the first multi-party ballot since General Sani Abacha seized power in November 1993.
The last time Nigerians voted to end the army's long stranglehold on power ended in fiasco. The military abruptly scrapped the June 1993 presidential poll as a winner emerged.
Abacha seized power in the confusion that ensued, but Nigeria plunged further into crisis after he jailed the presumed winner of the election, southern businessman Moshood Abiola.

Authorities gave a warning they would deal ruthlessly with anyone causing trouble at polling centres. Police units were standing by at police stations but there was no sign of security forces at polling stations.
No established international or Western monitoring groups have been invited to observe the elections although a 30-member U.S. team of mostly African Americans arrived this week.
The government has been shunned by Western powers since the 1995 hanging of writer Ken Saro Wiwa and eight other minority activists after a special court convicted them of murder.
But judging by the massive registration for the vote, the enthusiasm of Nigerians for elections has not diminished.
The National Electoral Commission of Nigeria (NECON) released final figures showing nearly 56 million voters had been registered for the poll from a population of about 100 million.
Pro-democracy groups, who denounce the military's democracy programme as a sham, urged people to ignore local elections held as a test run exactly a year ago on non-party basis.
This time they have not urged a boycott but neither have they shown any enthusiasm for the ballot.

Under Abacha's democracy programme, elections at state level will be held in the third quarter of the year. National elections are scheduled for next year, culminating in a presidential poll and the handover of power to an elected civilian president on October 1, 1998.
Speculation is rife that Abacha will contest next year's presidential election to turn himself into an elected leader.
